coach_says: Your bishop on f2 is attacked by the rook on f1 and only defended by your rook on a2, and White's other rook wants to come to f3 to hit it a second time. With your king on the f-file, Rf3 comes with check, so you never get time to save the bishop and lose it after R3xf2. Step the king off the f-file (Ke6, Kg6 or Ke5) so Rf3 is no longer check and you can move the bishop away.
concept: king on the same file as the loose bishop

coach_says: Your d6 pawn is attacked by the e5 pawn and, behind White's queen, by the rook on d1. Offering the queen trade with Qc6 takes away one of its defenders: after Qxc6 bxc6 exd6, you can't take back with the bishop because the d-file is now open and Rxd6 wins it, and then c5 falls too. Before trading, ask what the piece you are trading was defending; keep the queen guarding d6 with Qe8 or Qe6.
also: the d-file opens for White's rook

coach_says: White's d5 pawn was simply free: Qxd5 takes it, and if White trades queens you are two pawns up in a quiet position. After Bd6, White plays Nc3 and wins back your e4 pawn, so your extra pawn disappears. When you are ahead and a pawn is hanging, take it, especially when the trade of queens that follows suits you.
concept: missed a free pawn on d5

coach_says: You are already a pawn down, and c5 puts another pawn on a square nothing defends: Black's bishop on f8 just takes it with Bxc5 (after h6 and Bxf6 if Black wants). Before pushing a pawn, check who attacks and who defends the square it lands on. Developing with Bd3, which also guards e4, keeps your pieces working and your pawns safe.

White's queen on f5 and bishop on d3 both aim at h7, threatening Qh7+ Kf8 Qh8 mate, because your own queen blocks e7 and the king has nowhere to run. Grabbing the b2 pawn ignored that, and the mate came at once. When the opponent lines up a queen and bishop on your king, first ask what their next move threatens; g6, Kf8 or Qf6 would have stopped it.

Your knight on e5 is attacked twice, by the knight on f3 and the bishop on b2, and was defended twice, by your bishop and your queen on e7. Recapturing with the queen pulls it off e7, so Nxe5 wins the knight because Bxe5 Bxe5 leaves you a piece down. Kxd7 looks odd, but it keeps the queen guarding e5; before recapturing, check what the recapturing piece was protecting.

Nf3 attacks your e5 pawn, and Bc5 does nothing about it, so White just takes it with Nxe5. Black can sometimes chase the pawn back with the queen, but that brings your queen out early and White ends up better anyway. When a developing move attacks something, answer the threat first: Nc6 defends e5 and develops at the same time.

After Bxf3 Qxf3 White's queen arrives on f3 with a free hand on the light squares: it hits b7 and can jump to h5 with check, while the bishop on c4 already aims at your king. With your kingside pawns broken up, your light-squared bishop was the main defender of f7, g6 and h5. Keep it and the pin with Bh5 instead of trading it for the knight.

Rf4 attacks the bishop, but White just plays Bg3 and your rook has to move again, while White gets in Re8+ and Rad1 to go after your d3 pawn and the d4 bishop. Your bishop on c8 and rook on a8 are still at home, and your extra material depends on that strong d3 pawn. Moves like b6 and c5, then Ba6 or Bb7, get your pieces out and support the pawn instead of making a threat that is easily parried.
concept: lost time with a one-move threat

coach_says: Your queen had to move because the knight on d4 attacked it, but on f2 it can be hit again by Ng4, so you lose another move. Qd3 is better: it guards c2 against the knight fork and attacks the d4 knight itself, so Black has to respond to you. When your queen is attacked, look for a square that makes a threat of its own and can't be easily chased.
concept: retreat the queen with a threat

coach_says: Black is threatening Bc5 and then Qxf2 mate, because f2 is only defended by your king and your pieces are still at home. Bb5 does nothing about that, and you have to scramble with Rh2 after Bc5. Nc3 develops and attacks the e4 pawn, and if Black plays Bc5 then Nxe4 hits the queen and bishop and guards f2.

Black's queen on b3 is deep in your camp with very few safe squares. a5 takes away b6, gives your knight the b6 square to fork the a8 rook, and gets ready for Rfb1 to hunt the queen. Na5 attacks the queen but lets it escape with Qc3, offering a queen trade that takes the pressure off. When an enemy queen is short of squares, take its squares away first instead of just attacking it.

Nf6 is a fine developing move; the damage was done a move earlier with Bxf2+, which gave up a bishop for a pawn. From here just develop quickly, castle and look for chances against White's king, which Nf6 helps with.
Bd8 is about as good as anything here; your position was already difficult because of the d6 pawn and the open d-file. Keeping the bishop to blockade and fight the d-pawn is a sensible plan.
1...c5 is a perfectly good reply to 1.Nc3, taking space in the centre. Nothing to fix here.
Rc1 is the engine's top choice: you get your rook off the back rank where Black's bishop was hitting it and point it at the c7 pawn. The position was already hard; this was a good practical move.
g5 keeps your big advantage; the d7 pawn is still the key to the position. Bringing the rook to d1 to support it was a touch more precise, but you are winning either way.
The position is lost because of the f7 pawn about to queen, and Ne5 is as good a try as anything. There is nothing different to learn from this particular move.

Castling is sensible, but Black's king is stuck in the centre with broken kingside pawns, and that calls for action now. Nd4 attacks the f5 bishop and opens the way for Qh5+: if exd4, Qh5+ and Qxf5 wins the piece back with a strong attack. When the enemy king is exposed, look for checks and moves that hit loose pieces before making quiet moves.

When ...f6 attacked your bishop, retreating with Bf4 let Black play fxe5 and open the f-file for their rook. Capturing first was stronger: exf6 Bxf6 Bxf6 Rxf6, and then g4 kicks the f5 knight, which stands between your queen on f3 and the rook on f6, so you win the exchange. When a piece is attacked, check captures and pins before retreating.
